source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 2.2.6 heading and opening sentence: `Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent random variables.`
source_evidence.observation: The referenced result is Hoeffding's inequality for a finite family of independent random variables; identical distribution is not assumed.

source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 2.2.6 assumption: `Assume that X_i ∈ [m_i, M_i] for every i.`
source_evidence.observation: Each variable is bounded by its own interval with endpoints m_i and M_i.

source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 2.2.6 clause `Then, for any t > 0` and the displayed probability inequality immediately following it.
source_evidence.observation: For every positive t, the one-sided upper tail of the centered sum is bounded by exp(-2 t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N (M_i-m_i)^2).

source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.2.7: `Prove Theorem 2.2.6, possibly with some absolute constant instead of 2 in the tail.`
source_evidence.observation: The exercise permits proving the same tail estimate with an unspecified absolute constant replacing the coefficient 2 in the exponent.

binders: N, implicitly the positive integer indexing the finite family X_1, ..., X_N.
Independent real-valued random variables X_1, ..., X_N.
Real interval endpoints m_i and M_i for each i = 1, ..., N.
A real threshold t satisfying t > 0.

For the relaxation explicitly permitted by Exercise 2.2.7, some positive absolute numerical constant c, universal and independent of N, t, the variables, their distributions, and all interval endpoints.
hypotheses: The random variables X_1, ..., X_N are mutually independent.
For every i = 1, ..., N, X_i takes values in [m_i, M_i] (in standard probabilistic usage, this is an almost-sure bound).
The tail threshold t is strictly positive.
conclusions: Theorem 2.2.6 states P{sum_{i=1}^N (X_i - E X_i) >= t} <= exp(-2 t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N (M_i - m_i)^2).

For Exercise 2.2.7, it is also acceptable to establish P{sum_{i=1}^N (X_i - E X_i) >= t} <= exp(-c t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N (M_i - m_i)^2) for some positive absolute constant c in place of the displayed coefficient 2.
definitions_and_conventions: E X_i denotes the expectation of X_i, so each summand X_i - E X_i is centered.
P{...} denotes the probability of the displayed event.
The sum in the event and the sum of squared interval widths both run from i = 1 to N.
The displayed bound concerns only the upper tail of the centered sum, not an absolute-value or two-sided event.
An absolute constant is understood as a fixed universal numerical constant, not one depending on N, t, the variables, their laws, or the bounds m_i and M_i.
implicit_context: The theorem occurs in Section 2.2, Hoeffding's inequality, as the extension from symmetric Bernoulli variables to general bounded random variables.
Membership X_i ∈ [m_i, M_i] implicitly entails m_i <= M_i and boundedness sufficient for E X_i to exist.
No common distribution, common interval, zero-mean assumption, or symmetry assumption is imposed.

details: There are N random variables on a common probability space.
The required dependence condition is mutual independence.
The random sum is centered term by term using X_i - E X_i.
The event is the one-sided upper-deviation event that the centered sum is at least t.
The denominator is the sum of the squared individual interval widths (M_i - m_i)^2.
The exact theorem has exponential coefficient 2 multiplying t^2 in the negative exponent.
The exercise asks for a proof of Theorem 2.2.6 but expressly allows an absolute constant in place of 2 in the tail.
The natural substantive reading is existence of a positive universal coefficient c in the same exponent and with every other component of the theorem unchanged.

undebatable_constraints: The contracted claim must concern a finite family X_1, ..., X_N of independent bounded random variables.
Each X_i has its own source interval [m_i, M_i]; the variance proxy is exactly the sum of squared widths sum_{i=1}^N (M_i - m_i)^2.
The random expression is the centered sum sum_{i=1}^N (X_i - E X_i).
The event is a one-sided upper tail with threshold t > 0.
The exact Theorem 2.2.6 coefficient is 2 in exp(-2 t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N (M_i - m_i)^2).
For Exercise 2.2.7, replacing 2 by some positive absolute constant is explicitly permitted, but that constant must not depend on any problem data.

The exercise's permission changes only the absolute coefficient in the exponential tail rate; it does not license changing the centering, the squared-width denominator, independence, or the quantification over t > 0.

ambiguities.issue: The source uses `X_i ∈ [m_i, M_i]` without explicitly stating whether the bound is pointwise or almost sure.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 6; printed page 17, Theorem 2.2.6 assumption `Assume that X_i ∈ [m_i, M_i] for every i.`
ambiguities.impact: The usual probabilistic interpretation is almost-sure boundedness, but the printed sentence does not formalize the null-set convention.

ambiguities.issue: The all-degenerate case sum_{i=1}^N (M_i - m_i)^2 = 0 is not given a separate convention.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 6; printed page 17, the displayed denominator sum_{i=1}^N (M_i - m_i)^2 and the absence of an exceptional-case clause.
ambiguities.impact: Taken literally over ordinary real arithmetic, the displayed quotient is undefined when every interval has zero width; probabilistically the positive-threshold event is then impossible, but the source does not say how the formula itself is interpreted.

ambiguities.issue: The exercise does not formally quantify or specify the sign of `some absolute constant`.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 6; printed page 17, Exercise 2.2.7 phrase `possibly with some absolute constant instead of 2 in the tail.`
ambiguities.impact: The standard nontrivial reading is a fixed positive universal coefficient c replacing 2 in the negative exponent; allowing c = 0 would reduce the conclusion to the trivial probability bound by 1 and would not constitute the intended tail estimate.

contract_plain_english: Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent real-valued random variables, with each X_i bounded in its own interval [m_i, M_i]. For every t > 0, Theorem 2.2.6 bounds the probability that the centered sum sum_i (X_i - E X_i) is at least t by exp(-2 t^2 / sum_i (M_i - m_i)^2). Exercise 2.2.7 asks for a proof of this theorem and explicitly permits the coefficient 2 in the exponential tail to be replaced by some unspecified positive absolute constant that is universal and independent of all problem data.
